RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Langobards in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Lower Elbe Valley, merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Langobards was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Lower Elbe Valley, cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Behind the battle line the baggage train sinks axle-deep in sodden mud, and the handlers heave the wheels with their backs. Requisitioned rye has gone hard as granite, and the sergeant hands out each sack with a curse. Pay in salt or copper arrives late, so a man thanks the gods for it and hopes to strip silver from the enemy dead. At the Langobards post, the night watchword is "Iron."

At the manor gate, the reeve reckons the year: a tenth of the grain goes to the lord's barns, and three forges turned out two hundred horseshoes and eighty spearheads last month. Casks of olive oil sold at the spring fair will pay for the knights' mail. He seals a coded note for the port factor, because the price of iron in the markets is the lord's private business.
